SplicR for the Varmus lab
A549 LKB1 screens, revisited
Sahaj Satani, Pranav Mettu, Ishaan Samantray Cornell students
Slide 1: SplicR for the Varmus lab

Sahaj Satani, Pranav Mettu and Ishaan Samantray are Cornell students who built SplicR. This is a discussion of the lab's published A549 LKB1 CRISPR data and an actual deployed reanalysis. The Cornell affiliation identifies the students and does not imply institutional endorsement. Paper: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2403685121.

The paper’s biological question
How does LKB1 restrain lung cancer cell growth in spheroids?
02
The screen points to the PIKFYVE complex. Follow-up experiments connect it to how cells take in growth signals.
SplicR examines the CRISPR evidence behind that story.
Ferrarone et al., PNAS 2024, Fig. 4. Published experiment, not a SplicR output.
Slide 2: The paper’s biological question

Ferrarone et al., PNAS 2024, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2403685121. Full title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens in spheroid culture reveal that the tumor suppressor LKB1 inhibits growth via the PIKFYVE lipid kinase. LKB1 is a tumor suppressor. In this study restoring LKB1 restrains growth more strongly in spheroid culture. The screen and follow-up experiments implicate the PIKFYVE complex and growth factor receptor trafficking. The image is the authors' complete, unmodified Figure 4, used here to discuss their experiments. Red fluorescence reports internalized EGF, not a SplicR prediction. Panels D–F concern a mouse tumor cell line, not the uploaded A549 CRISPR count tables. Copyright 2024 the authors, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Keep the attribution with the image.

The screen design
A549 cells, TKOv3 knockout library, day 21
03
CultureLKB1-null (EV)LKB1-restored (WT)
2D monolayera and ba and b
3D spheroida and ba and b
One shared plasmid library reference
Eight endpoint samples. The plasmid reference is not a biological replicate.
Slide 3: The screen design

Paper: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2403685121. Dataset: https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/8DEPIT. A549 is a human lung adenocarcinoma cell line. EV is the empty-vector, LKB1-null arm. WT restores wild-type LKB1. Both culture conditions have two day-21 endpoint samples per arm, labeled a and b. The count tables share one identical plasmid library reference. It is neither a biological replicate nor a cellular day-zero sample. Two separate culture analyses do not establish a formal culture-by-genotype interaction. The TKOv3 library is Addgene 90294.

Slide 4: The deposited files pass identity checks

Source manifest and original archive metadata are in source-manifest.json and dataverse-metadata.json. MD5 and file sizes match Harvard Dataverse V1 exactly for both user downloads. The two tables contain the same 70,116 unique guide IDs and identical plasmid counts. Every observed guide matches the TKOv3 reference. The reference has 71,090 guides, so 974 reference guides are absent from these deposited tables. SplicR retains all deposited guide rows and does not fabricate missing rows. Each table contains 104 rows whose Gene label resembles an Excel date conversion. Joining exact guide IDs to TKOv3 restores reference gene labels, yielding 18,049 observed target labels. Those are the library's historical annotations, not a claim of current HGNC harmonization. Archive: https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/8DEPIT.

Upload the original count tables
05
Two files. No FASTQ download is needed for this count-table demo.
Slide 5: Upload the original count tables

Actual production upload at https://www.splicr.org. Sources: https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/8DEPIT. Download URLs: https://dataverse.harvard.edu/api/access/datafile/7440985 (2D) and https://dataverse.harvard.edu/api/access/datafile/7440983 (spheroid). The prepared ZIP contains the two original files with their bytes unchanged. The archive also contains eight FASTQ files. Reprocessing those would be a separate sequencing alignment analysis, requiring the original trimming/alignment settings and plasmid reference information. Upload inspection does not dispatch an analysis job. No new analysis was launched while capturing these screenshots.

SplicR identifies the guide library
06
All observed guide IDs match TKOv3. The mapping stays visible for review.
Slide 6: SplicR identifies the guide library

Actual production screenshot. The intake matches guide IDs against hosted TKOv3. Canonical library membership and complete row checks matter more than file-name guesses. The exact Ferrarone profile additionally requires both source checksums, the exact sample schemas and 70,116 rows. Renaming the same bytes preserves identity; modified bytes do not inherit this verified study profile. For other files, library candidates use evidence from guides or sampled sequences and ambiguous mappings require review. All 70,116 observed guide IDs match; 974 library reference guides are not in the deposited count files.

Six comparisons, ready to review
07
EV versus plasmid. WT versus plasmid. WT versus EV. Separately for each culture.
Slide 7: Six comparisons, ready to review

Actual production screenshot. The intake suggests six independent comparisons from the verified study profile. The two plasmid contrasts per culture are loss-of-function fitness comparisons. WT versus EV is a genotype contrast, not a drug contrast. The profile disables DrugZ for this experiment and does not pool 2D with spheroid samples. Researchers can edit names, selected samples and comparison definitions before launching. Culture-specific significance alone is not a formal interaction test. These comparisons are an explicitly declared reanalysis, not a recovery of unpublished original command lines.

Researchers control the analysis
08
Median normalization. FDR threshold 0.05. RRA with optional MLE. The reviewed plan travels with the run.
Slide 8: Researchers control the analysis

Actual configuration screenshot shows the default reviewed RRA+MLE plan. The candidate-count chart uses the separate RRA-only validation batch; the main completed report, export screenshot and reference-gene table use the full RRA+MLE batch. All six full RRA+MLE runs subsequently completed and their complete exports were verified. MLE uses a valid explicit baseline/treatment design, seed 0 and 10 permutation rounds in MAGeCK 0.5.9.5. The UI permits normalization and FDR customization, explicit MLE matrices and coefficients, optional BAGEL2 for compatible fitness comparisons and paired DrugZ for matched drug arms. BAGEL2, DrugZ, Chronos and copy-number correction are not part of this completed RRA demo. TKOv3 has no annotated non-targeting controls, so control-guide normalization requires an explicit suitable reference set.

Slide 9: Live progress follows recorded stages

Actual production screenshot of an existing full-genome MLE analysis. The progress bar records completed stages, not percentage of compute time or a promised finish time. This screenshot was captured during hit calling; all six full MLE runs have since completed. Some other existing MLE runs encountered count-write database timeouts and retried. Retry startup now resets stale stage records, and bulk writes use bounded COPY batches with a transaction-local timeout. Full MLE computation is complete; reconciliation with the authors’ settings and nomination criteria remains open. Frontend realtime events and a five-second polling fallback read Supabase run and stage records. Cloudflare R2 stores input objects, Supabase stores metadata and results, and Modal executes analysis. The screenshot is a dated snapshot. No new analysis job was submitted for this presentation.

A completed report exposes uncertainty
Spheroid WT versus plasmid, completed RRA + MLE run
10
178 candidates. 172 flagged for review, not automatic rejection.
176 depleted. 154 annotated pan-essential in DepMap, consistent with common survival dependencies.
Slide 10: A completed report exposes uncertainty

Actual production full RRA+MLE report for spheroid WT versus plasmid. The primary candidate count uses RRA, with MLE statistics retained separately. 18,049 genes have recorded statistics. 178 pass the SplicR two-direction FDR threshold 0.05, of which 172 have at least one artifact flag. Flags prompt inspection and do not automatically disprove a gene. Of these 178 RRA candidates, 176 are depleted and 2 enriched. 154 carry the stored DepMap pan-essential flag, consistent with many general survival dependencies in a plasmid comparison. Another 16 carry an Atlas recurring-hit flag. Flag categories overlap: 170 frequent hitters, 58 promiscuous-guide flags and 44 multi-site-guide flags. Their sum is not a count of distinct genes. Common dependency annotations are context, not proof of the mechanism in this experiment. The WT-versus-EV endpoint comparison addresses relative abundance under LKB1 restoration and must be interpreted with its own quality and statistical limits. QC warns about replicate disagreement and count skew. No gene has recorded bench validation in this workspace. Numerical completion is not biological validation. All six completed RRA reports passed live API and browser export checks.

Slide 11: Results across the six comparisons

Data: rra-cloud/comparison-summary.csv. Each comparison scores 18,049 genes. Counts at SplicR's two-direction FDR <= 0.05 are 205,271,0,159,178,0 for 2D EV/plasmid, 2D WT/plasmid, 2D WT/EV, spheroid EV/plasmid, spheroid WT/plasmid and spheroid WT/EV, respectively. SplicR preserves both MAGeCK directional FDRs and reports min(1,2*min(q_depleted,q_enriched)) as a conservative union bound. This differs from independently counting either native directional FDR below 0.05. The chart is a result of the declared RRA configuration, not a reproduction of the authors' MLE beta-score figure. All six reports carry QC warnings. Zero significant genes in a WT versus EV comparison does not establish absence of a biological effect.

Positive effects and significance are different questions
None passes MLE FDR 0.05 here. The paper’s beta-score nomination uses different criteria.
Slide 12: The paper’s genes, across both methods

Completed full RRA+MLE run, spheroid WT versus plasmid: FIG4 RRA log2 fold change 3.1413, MLE beta 1.8331 and MLE FDR 0.57554; VAC14 LFC 4.9627, beta 3.211 and FDR 0.19162; PIKFYVE LFC 0.40606, beta 0.43846 and FDR 0.99966. Values rounded only for display. None passes the declared RRA or MLE FDR threshold 0.05 here. Spheroid EV-versus-plasmid MLE beta values are FIG4 1.1152, VAC14 -0.031009 and PIKFYVE 0.37959. VAC14 meets both published WT-enriched/EV-low beta thresholds, but FIG4 does not meet their EV-low cutoff in this separately fitted design. The paper’s methods use WT beta >0.5 / EV <0.5 for pathway analysis; its Figure 3 caption uses >1 / <1. Both cutoff passages describe pathway-analysis input for Figure 3D, not FDR significance criteria for the entire screen. The actual implemented rule is not established by these descriptions. Ask which rule generated Figure 3D without assuming a typo or treating the difference as evidence against the biological conclusions. Original normalization, guide filtering and the design also need investigator clarification. The authors used MLE beta nomination and wet-lab follow-up; beta criteria and FDR calls are different evidence criteria. PIKFYVE guides were not enriched in WT spheroids in the paper, and pharmacological/rescue experiments established its role. These results do not establish exact reproduction or superior biology. Sources: full reference-gene-statistics.csv and https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2403685121.

Actual screenshot of the recorded report's provenance and export controls. The CSV was downloaded by clicking the production UI, and its contents include all 18,049 gene rows with source/run metadata and separate RRA and MLE fields. The full run includes complete separate RRA and MLE statistics for every scored gene. Older RRA-only exports keep unavailable MLE fields blank, not zero. RRA timing shown. Initial full MLE cohort: 5 h 5 min, including retries. Upload time excluded.
Slide 14: Measured runtime and reproducibility

Cloud receipts record six RRA jobs with worker durations 123.091,107.553,107.435,96.616,126.319,110.712 seconds. The first worker started 2026-10-07T16:22:43.148Z and the final worker finished 16:28:45.299Z, giving 362.151 seconds (6 minutes 2 seconds after rounding). This is elapsed worker cohort time and excludes upload/inspection and pre-start waiting. These jobs used the count-table pipeline, not raw FASTQ alignment, and excluded MLE. The initial full MLE cohort subsequently completed in 18,316.696 elapsed seconds (5 hours 5 minutes), including retries and its original worker allocation. This is a separate method/runtime, not the six-minute RRA result. It excludes upload and pre-start waiting. Independent local RRA matched cloud LFC, both native directional FDRs and union FDR across all 18,049 genes in every comparison with maximum absolute difference 0. This establishes numerical reproducibility for the declared inputs/configuration, not accuracy against biological truth. The authors do not report a comparable compute runtime, so no speed multiple against them is claimed.

Slide 15: SplicR alongside Broad Apron

Primary sources checked 2026-10-07: Broad's post-screen page https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gpp/public/resources/post-screen and Apron guide https://docs.google.com/document/d/14ry2-S3zWCwJVZzxS2QLSdNGqyl6QaFK7rhkcyh7jXU/preview. Apron is a guided web app with QC, replicate exploration, plots and downloadable gene lists. It is optimized for PoolQ counts with .chip annotations and supports other formatted inputs. Its documented target aggregation uses Stouffer z-scores and an empirical null from control constructs. Its guide supports manual reference and replicate definitions and multiple data configurations. SplicR's tested Ferrarone flow adds exact source identification, guide-ID annotation repair and automatic six-comparison suggestions. SplicR uses MAGeCK RRA plus optional MLE, preserving separate statistics. These are workflow differences, not an experimentally measured accuracy or usability victory. We did not run Apron on these files or benchmark its runtime. The Broad GPP page documents CRISPRko/a/i with Cas9/Cas12a for single-gene constructs, broader than the Cas9 knockout evidence in this particular demo.

Slide 16: Other tools and SplicR’s role

Sources: official MAGeCK documentation https://sourceforge.net/p/mageck/wiki/usage/ and the original PinAPL-Py paper https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-017-16193-9. MAGeCK offers mature RRA/MLE analysis and explicit design matrices via command line. PinAPL-Py already offers a web interface, automated adapter-based guide extraction, custom libraries, QC and adjustable ranking. The comparison describes those published capabilities and does not establish that their hosted services are currently operational. SplicR's implemented role is a shared research workflow around established statistical methods with source recognition, reviewable configuration, guide-level evidence and saved receipts. Interface convenience, model prediction, statistical significance and biological validation are different dimensions. No head-to-head performance or accuracy ranking was performed.

A reusable workflow for other labs
17
Researchers can change sample roles, replicates and factors. Their experiment determines the configuration.
Slide 17: A reusable workflow for other labs

Actual editable sample-metadata screenshot. Tested customization includes custom uploaded guide libraries, correction of selected count columns, donors, replicate labels, dates, researcher attribution, saved draft resumption and FASTQ reads with adapter prefixes. Backend validation checks treatment/control selections, matched replicate requirements for paired DrugZ, normalization controls, MLE design rank and selected coefficients. The exact Ferrarone profile is a special verified study profile, while the generic intake uses evidence-based suggestions and review. This demonstration validates human Cas9 knockout pooled abundance counts; it does not validate every organism, modality or assay. Base editing, multi-gene combinatorial perturbations, single-cell readouts and spatial assays need dedicated models and separate validation. Chronos and copy-number correction are unavailable in this intake because required metadata/profiles are not supplied.

Slide 18: A pilot with the Varmus lab

Proposed next step for discussion, not a commitment from the lab. Ask the investigators to confirm original normalization, guide filtering, MLE design, permutation settings and complete output tables. Compare a frozen SplicR run to a frozen reference workflow on agreed genes and statistics. Evaluate whether differences are expected methodological effects or defects. Measure analyst time and review burden directly rather than estimating historical authors' work. Choose one new screen with known positive/negative controls and a small follow-up validation set. Prospective validation, not a polished dashboard, determines scientific benefit. No investigator was emailed and no new analysis job was queued for this deck.

Methods and scientific limits

Slide 19: Methods and scientific limits

Sources: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2403685121, https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/8DEPIT, https://sourceforge.net/p/mageck/wiki/usage/. Reanalysis uses deposited count tables, exact TKOv3 guide-ID annotation, MAGeCK 0.5.9.5, median normalization, RRA union FDR threshold 0.05. It retains all deposited guide rows and does not recreate the authors' Cutadapt/Bowtie processing or unspecified implementation of the read-count <30 filter. Authors' methods describe that filter but not which samples define it. MLE runs use explicit baseline-first design, seed 0, 10 permutation rounds and grouped permutations. We did not reduce permutation rounds to claim a faster run. Copy-number correction, Chronos, BAGEL2 and DrugZ are off in this study's completed RRA cohort. Core essential separation supports count-table fitness QC, but replicate disagreement and skew remain warnings. Count tables cannot establish sequencing mapping efficiency. Atlas uses previous-screen evidence to describe recurring hits. That context does not independently validate this study's candidates. The saved receipt records a publication exclusion policy for benchmark holdouts, but it does not establish that this specific paper was held out. The validation network has no fitted outcomes cohort on this deployed worker and refuses probabilities with a reason. Missing predictions and absent methods must stay unavailable. Separate WT/EV culture tests do not establish a culture interaction.
